source.origins: Johnson, J. A. (2019). Populating the periodic table: Nucleosynthesis of the elements. Science 363(6426), 474-478. Simplified to each element's leading sources.

conventions.width: Van der Waals diameter (2x the radius): how close two atoms sit before their electron clouds push back. The same convention as the oxygen and helium atoms on the main chart.
conventions.mass: Standard atomic weight, or the mass of the longest-lived isotope when there is no stable one.
conventions.first_appeared: When the element's first neutral atoms existed: the earliest of its sources. Times for stellar sources are rough (the first stars formed ~100-200 million years in).
conventions.same_as: The main-chart object that already is this element's atom; show that instead of a second dot.

sources.label: The Big Bang
sources.description: Nuclei formed in the first few minutes; atoms once the universe cooled enough to hold electrons.

sources.label: Cosmic rays splitting heavier nuclei
sources.description: Made when cosmic rays from supernova remnants shatter carbon, nitrogen and oxygen.

sources.label: Exploding massive stars
sources.description: Forged in massive stars and spread by their supernovae, the first ~200 million years after the Big Bang.

sources.label: Dying low-mass stars
sources.description: Made by slow neutron capture (the s-process) in red giants and shed as they die.

sources.label: Exploding white dwarfs
sources.description: Made in thermonuclear (type Ia) supernovae, which need a white dwarf and a partner.

sources.label: Merging neutron stars
sources.description: Made by rapid neutron capture (the r-process) in neutron-star mergers and perhaps rare supernovae.

sources.label: Decay of uranium and thorium
sources.description: Every isotope is short-lived; it exists in nature only as it is continually made by uranium and thorium decaying.

sources.label: Made in laboratories
sources.description: Not found in nature; made one atom at a time in accelerators or reactors.
